entry: Military or paramilitary force of civilian members rather than a professional standing army of regular, full-time personnel. Militias may be raised in times of need to support regular troops or to serve as a pool of manpower for them. Acting alone, they are generally unable to hold ground against regular forces, so they commonly skirmish, hold fortifications or conduct irregular warfare, though they may also defend a community's territory, property and laws. Since the late 20th century, some officially recognized militias have operated as professional but part-time forces; members of the [[United States]] National Guard, for instance, are trained to the same standards as full-time soldiers. Under [[Conscription|conscription]], the term may refer to the entire able-bodied population available for military service. In [[Russia]] and some countries of the former [[Soviet Union]], an official reserve army of citizen soldiers is known as the militsiya.

Species of ray-finned fish found throughout the Indo-Pacific, the sole living species in the family Chanidae. The milkfish (*Chanos chanos*) is the only living member of its genus, and its tautonym derives from Greek *khanos*, meaning mouth. It is most closely related to the Ostariophysi, a group that includes [[Carp|carps]] and [[Catfish|catfish]]. Milkfish occur in the [[Indian Ocean]] and across the [[Pacific Ocean]], typically in tropical offshore waters around islands and along continental shelves, and they often enter estuaries and rivers. Most are no longer than 1 m (39 in), though they can reach 1.80 m (5 ft 11 in). The body is olive green with silvery flanks, and the mouth is small and toothless. Milkfish are widely farmed in ponds, particularly in [[Southeast Asia]]. In the [[Philippines]], where the fish is called bangús, it is popularly considered the national fish, although the National Commission for Culture and the Arts has stated that this has no basis in Philippine law.

Demographic cohort following [[Generation X]] and preceding [[Generation Z]], generally defined as people born from 1981 to 1996. Also called Generation Y, millennials saw the rise of the [[Information Age]] and the [[Internet]] as children, and as young adults they used early social media such as AOL Instant Messenger and Myspace. Many have faced high youth unemployment, student debt and childcare costs after the [[Great Recession]] and the COVID-19 recession, and they have been called the "Unluckiest Generation" in the United States. Millennials have postponed marriage and continue to have fewer children than their predecessors.

Seven unsolved mathematical problems, each with a prize of one million US dollars for a correct solution. Selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, they were inspired by [[David Hilbert]]'s 1900 problems and include the [[Riemann hypothesis]], [[P versus NP problem|P versus NP]] and the [[Poincaré conjecture]]. As of 2026, only the Poincaré conjecture has been officially declared solved; the institute awarded its prize to Grigori Perelman in 2010, but he declined it. In September 2026, OpenAI presented a proposed counterexample to the Navier–Stokes problem, but the claim has yet to be verified by the independent mathematical community.

Highly varied group of small-seeded grasses grown as a staple [[Cereal|cereal]] crop. Most millets belong to the tribe Paniceae of the [[Poaceae|grass family]], and they are used both as food for humans and as fodder for [[Livestock|livestock]]. Millets are highly tolerant of drought and have a short growing season under hot, dry conditions, which suits the semi-arid tropics of Asia and Africa, especially India, Mali, Nigeria and Niger. They account for 97% of agricultural output in developing countries. Pearl millet is the most commonly cultivated millet, although the term sometimes includes the widely cultivated [[Sorghum|sorghum]]. Humans may have consumed millets for about 7,000 years, and they may have had "a pivotal role in the rise of multi-crop agriculture and settled farming societies."

Arthropod of the class Diplopoda, with two pairs of jointed legs on most body segments. The name comes from [[Latin]] *mille*, meaning thousand, and *pes*, meaning foot, but no species was known to have 1,000 or more legs until the 2020 discovery of *Eumillipes persephone*, which can have over 1,300. Each double-legged segment results from two fused segments. There are about 12,000 named species in 16 orders, making millipedes the largest class of [[Myriapoda]]. Most are slow-moving detritivores that feed on decaying leaves and other dead plant matter. Most defend themselves with chemicals secreted from body pores, and many curl into a tight coil. Reproduction in most species is carried out by modified male legs called gonopods. First appearing in the [[Silurian]] period, millipedes are among the oldest known land animals. Unlike the faster, venomous and carnivorous [[Centipede|centipedes]], they are generally harmless to humans.

American economist and statistician. Friedman received the 1976 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his research on consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and the complexity of stabilization policy. Among the intellectual leaders of the Chicago school of economics, he challenged Keynesian theory and promoted monetarism, arguing that a steady, small expansion of the money supply was preferable to rapid and unexpected changes. He predicted what came to be known as stagflation. His 1962 book *Capitalism and Freedom* advocated a volunteer military, freely floating exchange rates, a negative income tax and school vouchers. He advised [[Ronald Reagan]] and [[Margaret Thatcher]], and his monetary theory influenced [[Federal Reserve]] policy after the [[2008 financial crisis]]. His 1975 visit to Chile, which included a meeting with [[Augusto Pinochet]], drew criticism for the regime's political repression.

City in [[Buckinghamshire]], England (pop., 2021: 264,349), about 50 miles (80 km) north-west of [[London]]. Designated a new town in the 1960s to relieve housing congestion in London, it was planned for 250,000 people. Its planners laid out a grid of distributor roads about 1 km (0.6 mi) apart, with shared-use paths for cyclists and pedestrians, and rejected the residential [[Tower block|tower block]] by setting a height limit of three storeys outside the central area. About 25% of the urban area is parkland or woodland, and the city is among the most economically productive in the UK.

Most populous city in [[Wisconsin]], on the western shore of [[Lake Michigan]] (pop., 2020: 577,222). Developed as an inland port after the 1833 Treaty of Chicago, it became a center of German American culture and a national leader in [[Beer|beer]] production in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when it also developed a sewer socialism movement. Its metropolitan area has over 1.57 million residents. The city is home to the headquarters of several Fortune 500 companies, including Northwestern Mutual and Rockwell Automation, as well as the motorcycle manufacturer Harley-Davidson. Its major professional teams are the Milwaukee Brewers and the Milwaukee Bucks.

Ottoman chief architect, engineer and mathematician for sultans [[Suleiman the Magnificent|Suleiman the Magnificent]], Selim II and Murad III. The son of a stonemason, he trained as a military engineer and rose through the ranks of the [[Janissary]] corps to become a commander. At about the age of fifty he was appointed chief royal architect, a post he held for almost fifty years. He was responsible for more than 300 major structures, including the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne, considered his masterpiece, and the Suleiman Mosque in [[Istanbul]], his most famous work. His apprentices later designed the Sultan Ahmed Mosque in Istanbul and the Stari Most bridge in Mostar. He is considered the greatest architect of the classical period of Ottoman architecture and has been compared to [[Michelangelo]], his contemporary in the West.

Performer who uses mime, or pantomime, as a theatrical medium or performance art. Mime originated in [[Ancient Greece]], where the first recorded mime was Telestēs in the play *Seven Against Thebes* by [[Aeschylus]]. It was an aspect of Roman theatre from its earliest times and became the predominant Roman drama under the [[Roman Empire]]; it was distinguished by its absence of masks and by female as well as male performers. In early nineteenth-century Paris, Jean-Gaspard Deburau established the silent figure in whiteface. Étienne Decroux developed corporeal mime into a highly sculptural form, and Jacques Lecoq contributed significantly to mime and physical theatre training. Mime has been on France's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage elements since 2017.

Genus of about 600 species of herbs and shrubs in the mimosoid clade of the legume family [[Fabaceae]]. Species are native to the [[Americas]], to eastern Africa, and to the Indian subcontinent and Indochina. The generic name derives from Greek *mimos*, meaning actor or mime, and refers to the "sensitive leaves" that seem to "mimic conscious life." *Mimosa pudica*, or touch-me-not, folds its leaves when touched or exposed to heat; it is widely cultivated as a houseplant and outdoors in the tropics, where it has become a weed in some areas, including [[Hawaii]]. *Mimosa tenuiflora* is used in shamanic [[Ayahuasca|ayahuasca]] brews for the psychedelic drug dimethyltryptamine in its root bark. Experiments on mimosas by Jean-Jacques d'Ortous de Mairan in 1729 provided the first evidence of biological clocks. Mimosas can be distinguished from the related genus [[Acacia]] because their flowers have ten or fewer stamens.

Primary branch of Sinitic languages, spoken in southern China and [[Taiwan]]. Min is a group of mutually unintelligible languages with about 75 million native speakers. They are spoken in a region centered on [[Fujian]] Province, from southern Zhejiang to eastern Guangdong, and on Hainan Island, as well as in Taiwan and by a large diaspora in [[Southeast Asia]]. The most widely spoken variety outside China is Hokkien, a form of Southern Min that originated in southern Fujian. Min languages have retained features of Old Chinese that were lost in other branches. Linguists estimate that the oldest layers of Min diverged from the rest of Chinese around the time of the [[Han dynasty]]. In 909, following the fall of the [[Tang dynasty]], Wang Shenzhi founded the Min Kingdom, one of the Ten Kingdoms of the [[Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period]].

State in southeastern [[Brazil]] (pop., 2022: 20,539,989), the fourth largest state by area and the second largest by population. Its name means General Mines, and its capital is [[Belo Horizonte]]. Gold discovered in the late 17th century drew a large migration and brought wealth to the colonial captaincy, until the gold became scarce and much of the population emigrated. A later coffee boom restored the state's national prominence, and the end of that cycle led to relatively late industrialization. Today the state has the third largest GDP among Brazilian states, and mining remains a large part of its economy. It has the largest road network in the country and many hydroelectric plants, and it is the source of several of Brazil's main rivers, including the São Francisco. Its colonial towns, such as Ouro Preto and Diamantina, are major tourist destinations.

Philosophical view that mental phenomena are non-physical, or that mind and body are distinct and separable. It is contrasted with [[Materialism|physicalism]], [[Monism|monism]] and enactivism in the mind–body problem. [[Plato]] held that the soul was not dependent on the physical body and believed in metempsychosis, the migration of the soul to a new body. [[Aristotle]] described a hierarchy of souls, of which only the intellective part of mind was immortal. Dualism is most closely associated with [[René Descartes]], who in *Meditations on First Philosophy* (1641) held that the mind is a nonphysical, non-spatial substance and identified it with consciousness and self-awareness. Most substance dualists hold that mind and body can causally affect each other, a view called interactionism. Critics argue that dualism cannot explain how an immaterial mind affects a physical body.

Second-largest island in the [[Philippines]], after [[Luzon]], in the southern part of the archipelago. It is part of an island group that includes the Sulu Archipelago. Mindanao had a population of 26,252,442 at the 2020 census and is divided into six administrative regions, including the autonomous region of Bangsamoro. [[Davao City]] is the most populous city, with 1,848,947 people at the 2024 census. Most residents identify as Christian, while [[Islam]] is the largest minority religion, although reports on religious demographics are often considered unreliable. The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is the most predominantly Islamic region, with above 89% of its population identifying as Muslim in the 2020 census. In the classic period, Hindu and Buddhist influence reached the island from [[Indonesia]] and [[Malaysia]]. Mindanao is considered the major breadbasket of the Philippines.

Sandbox video game developed and published by Mojang Studios, first released for [[Personal computer|personal computers]] on November 18, 2011. Players explore a procedurally generated world of three-dimensional blocks, or voxels, which they mine, craft and place to build structures, and they can fight hostile mobs or cooperate and compete in multiplayer. The game has no required goals, and its large community produces modifications, servers and custom maps. Originally created by Markus Persson, known as Notch, using [[Java (programming language)|Java]], it was acquired by [[Microsoft]] in 2014 for US$2.5 billion. It is the best-selling video game of all time, with over 400 million copies sold. The film adaptation *A Minecraft Movie* was released in 2025.

Branch of [[Geology|geology]] concerned with the chemistry, crystal structure and physical properties of minerals and mineralized artifacts. It also studies how minerals form, how they are classified, where they occur and how they are used. Early writing on minerals, especially on gemstones, came from Babylonia, the Greco-Roman world, China, India and the Islamic world. [[Pliny the Elder]]'s *Natural History* described many minerals and their properties. The modern discipline grew out of [[Crystallography|crystallography]] and the microscopic study of rock sections. In 1814 [[Jöns Jacob Berzelius]] introduced a classification of minerals based on their chemistry rather than their crystal structure. In 1912 Max von Laue demonstrated [[X-ray|X-ray]] diffraction, which was developed into a tool for analyzing crystal structure by [[William Henry Bragg]] and William Lawrence Bragg. Today the field overlaps with [[Materials science]] and solid-state physics.

Imperial dynasty of China (1368–1644), the last imperial dynasty ruled by the Han people. It followed the collapse of the Mongol-led [[Yuan dynasty]]. Its founder, the [[Hongwu Emperor]] (r. 1368–1398), sought to create rigid, self-sufficient rural communities that would support a permanent class of soldiers. The [[Yongle Emperor]] moved the capital to [[Beijing]], built the [[Forbidden City]] and restored the [[Grand Canal (China)|Grand Canal]]. [[Zheng He]] led seven voyages into the Indian Ocean as far as Arabia and the eastern coasts of Africa. Through European trade, the [[Columbian exchange]] introduced chili peppers, maize and potatoes, and South American silver re-monetized the economy. The dynasty collapsed in 1644 as the rebel forces of Li Zicheng entered Beijing, and Southern Ming regimes survived until 1662.

Movement in art and design that emphasizes reducing works to their essentials, focusing on the object itself and the viewer's experience. It emerged in Western art after World War II and is often interpreted as a reaction to [[Abstract expressionism]] and [[Modernism]]. In visual art, minimalism emerged in [[New York City|New York]] in the early 1960s, typically in simple geometric sculptures made of industrial materials such as plastic, metal, aluminum and concrete. Donald Judd's work was shown in 1964 at the Green Gallery in Manhattan. Minimal music, as in the works of [[Philip Glass]], features repetition and gradual variation. The term is also used for the plays and novels of [[Samuel Beckett]] and the films of [[Robert Bresson]].

Decision rule for minimizing the possible loss in a worst-case scenario, used in [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]], [[Game theory|game theory]], statistics and philosophy. When dealing with gains it is called maximin, which maximizes the minimum gain. Originally formulated for several-player [[Zero-sum game|zero-sum games]], it covers games with alternating and simultaneous moves and has been extended to decision-making under uncertainty. The minimax algorithm in artificial intelligence explores game trees to choose moves that assume perfect opponent play, as in [[Tic-tac-toe]].

City in Hennepin County, Minnesota, and the state's most populous city (pop., 2020: 429,954). It occupies both banks of the [[Mississippi River]] and adjoins Saint Paul, the state capital; together with the surrounding area, they form the Twin Cities metropolitan area. Dakota people inhabited the site before European settlement grew around Saint Anthony Falls, the only natural waterfall on the Mississippi. For a time in the 19th century, Minneapolis was the lumber and flour milling capital of the world. It is home to a [[Federal Reserve]] bank and is the birthplace of [[Target Corporation]], General Mills and the Pillsbury brand. Musician [[Prince (musician)|Prince]] played at the First Avenue nightclub, and the city is nicknamed the "City of Lakes" for its thirteen lakes.

U.S. state in the Upper Midwest, admitted to the Union as the 32nd state in 1858. Known as the "Land of 10,000 Lakes", it has 14,420 bodies of fresh water covering at least ten acres each. More than 60% of its roughly 5.8 million residents live in the [[Minneapolis]]–Saint Paul metropolitan area. Its name derives from the Dakota language, and its motto, *L'Étoile du Nord*, is the only state motto in French. Into the early 20th century, immigrants from [[Scandinavia]] and [[Germany]] arrived in large numbers. Minnesota has voted for every Democratic presidential nominee since 1976, longer than any other state.

Bronze Age culture centered on the island of [[Crete]] and other Aegean islands, often regarded as the first civilization in [[Europe]]. The Minoans traded extensively, exporting agricultural products and luxury crafts in exchange for raw metals, and their influence reached the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean. The civilization developed from the local [[Neolithic]] culture around 3100 BC. After c. 1450 BC it came under the cultural and perhaps political domination of the mainland Mycenaean Greeks. Largely forgotten after the [[Late Bronze Age collapse]], it was rediscovered through [[Archaeological excavation|archaeological excavation]] in the early 20th century. Neither of the two Minoan writing systems, Cretan hieroglyphs and Linear A, has been fully deciphered, so the language is unknown. The ruins of the Minoan palaces at [[Knossos]] and Phaistos are popular tourist attractions.

Astronomical object in direct orbit around the Sun that is classified as neither a planet nor a [[Comet|comet]]. Minor planets include [[Asteroid|asteroids]], [[Centaur|centaurs]] and trans-Neptunian objects, most of which lie in the [[Kuiper belt]] and the scattered disc. The first minor planet discovered was [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]] in 1801, though it was then called a planet. Since 2006 the International Astronomical Union has preferred the term small Solar System body, and objects large enough to achieve hydrostatic equilibrium are classified as [[Dwarf planet|dwarf planets]]. As of June 2026, there are 1,544,016 known minor planets, of which 895,910 are numbered. Unlike the eight official planets, minor planets fail to clear their orbital neighborhoods.
